results.title: GALLERY: Young stars take the reins at Tri-Nations rodeo
“ODIs can thrive”: ICC CEO Sanjog Gupta calls for end to random bilateral scheduling
results.description: ICC CEO Sanjog Gupta addressed the future of One Day Internationals (ODIs), emphasizing that the era of "randomly scheduled" bilateral cricket series must end to protect the sport's long-term sustainability. Gupta’s comments came a month after the ICC introduced a new 2027 World Cup format featuring a preliminary "Super Series" round. Cricket Scotland and Royal Dutch Cricket Association (KNCB) recently issued a joint statement, calling the World Cup format changes "disappointing and disrespectful". The controversial Super Series forces the 12th, 13th, and 14th ranked teams into a preliminary tri-series where only one team advances, which emerging boards view as a severe barrier to global growth. “The era of randomly scheduled bilateral series has to come to an end, because countries will not be able to sustain cricket without context, culture, competition and competitiveness, which require significant investment of resources, both financial and non-financial,” Gupta told PTI . “It’s important to stay focused on the four levers which drive attention and affiliation - context, culture, competition and competitiveness - and ODIs can continue not just to survive, but thrive. “There is a place for the format in the product portfolio, which is inextricably linked to men’s and women’s ICC Cricket World Cups. We need to look at what we want the format to stand for and how we want it to evolve, including the expanse of participation,” he added. Gupta argued that Test cricket must balance its heritage with commercial viability and optimal scheduling. He advocated for a growth-first mindset across all formats, citing that tradition should not override economic reality. “Our ambition has to be growth; our ambition should never be to maintain the status quo,” Gupta said. “Because in this world, where population is growing, attention is getting disaggregated and affiliation is hard to sustain, if you’re not growing, you’re dying.” “Every time there is conversation around the commercials of Test cricket, the passion, pride and legacy tend to override the conversation around the economics,” he stated. “I don’t think the answer is necessarily binary, and I don’t think it’s a question solely for Test cricket to answer but one which must be asked of all our products across formats and events. “Our primary tool of global growth is T20 cricket, but that does not mean we don’t focus on growing the value or engagement around ODIs or Test cricket. The World Test Championship Final is now an event of significance and one that didn’t even exist seven years ago,” he remarked. Sanjog Gupta stressed the need to revamp Test cricket scheduling outside the "Big Three" nations (India, England, and Australia) to make the format more appealing to the fans. “Test matches in certain countries are of immense fan value, but can we focus more on providing Members with opportunities to build occasions of appointment and significance in Test cricket? “That has to be by virtue of the World Test Championship having more meaning and a continuing narrative, by virtue of Test cricket being scheduled optimally, by virtue of Tests receiving adequate positioning and marketing support, by virtue of the competitive standards of the two teams and playing conditions being offered, and fans being promised cricket which is going to be compelling,” he said.

results.title: “I see it as a huge positive,” R Ashwin hails Ireland's recent 2-0 T20I series win over India
results.description: Dublin Guardians captain and mentor Ravichandran Ashwin praised Ireland's recent 2-0 T20I series win over India ahead of the inaugural European T20 Premier League (ETPL). The former India spinner cited that Ireland's triumph over the reigning T20 world champions underlined the competitive possibilities for emerging cricketing nations, while also highlighting how helpful balanced surfaces can be for bowlers in the shortest format. “Two things made me very happy. One was that a team ranked 10th could beat a team ranked first. I think the sport should be like that. It is also a lesson that the FIFA World Cup has taught us. For this game to become a truly global sport, with more nations coming to the fore and with cricket set to feature in the Olympics in the next couple of years, I see it as a huge positive,” Ashwin told JioStar . Ashwin noted that balanced pitches allow bowlers to compete fairly, proving that surface conditions are vital for an engaging contest between bat and ball. “The second aspect is that if there is something in the pitch and there is a balance between bat and ball, bowlers are going to come into play, which Ireland proved beyond any doubt,” he added. Ashwin commended Irish spinner Matthew Humphreys for dismissing Shivam Dube with finger spin against India, citing it as proof that the art remains relevant. “To have a left-arm spinner like Humphreys bowl to Shivam Dube and get him caught at square leg is a lesson for people who ask me what has happened to the art of finger spin,” he stated. Ashwin emphasized that modern T20 pitches heavily favor batters and bowlers need detailed game plans and a strong element of luck to survive because anyone can concede many runs on a given day. “The pitches have reached a point where any bowler can go the distance on a given day. I think you need a lot of luck to survive, apart from having plenty of plans in place in modern T20 cricket,” he remarked. Ashwin further praised Humphreys for handling late-over pressure. “So, it was a refreshing pitch to watch, and it was even more refreshing to see Humphreys being trusted with the 18th or 19th over against a left-hander. The pitch had enough in it and did not allow the left-hander to hit through the line. So, on both counts, it was very, very pleasing to watch,” he said. Ashwin will now shift his attention to the ETPL, where the Dublin Guardians are among the teams preparing for the league's first season. Rahul Dravid, the co-owner of the Dublin Guardians, praised Ashwin's cricketing legacy and his clear vision for mentoring young players during this stage of his career. “I'm glad that we got Ashwin on board. He is obviously a legend of the game and a world-class performer, but he is also a really good captain and leader. He is someone who has a very clear idea and vision of how, at this stage of his career, he wants to focus on developing and working with young talent,” Dravid said. (With IANS Inputs)
